transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-03-18 15:00 PT | Duration: 42m | Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Jordan (Redwood Product), Sara (Acme Head Eng), Mike (Acme ML Eng), Lina (Acme Security), Ben (Acme PM)

[00:00] Alex: hey everyone, thanks for joining, can you hear me okay?
[00:03] Sara: yeah loud and clear, thanks Alex.
[00:05] Alex: great, quick agenda — we'll do a 20-ish minute walkthrough of structured output + function calling (json mode), show the console demo, then go into Optimize suggestions for production, and leave time for Q&A and security questions. sound good?
[00:16] Mike: yep that's perfect. we're especially interested in reliably getting structured JSON back — we have a lot of downstream plumbing that expects precise fields.
[00:24] Priya: totally, we'll focus on schema enforcement, validators, and guardrails — how Redwood enforces shape, how function-calling works for deterministic actions, and how you can monitor regressions. note: some of the transcript may have typos, apologies in advance.
[00:37] [screen share starts]
[00:40] Priya: ok first slide, quick recap: Redwood supports structured output through two main modes: (1) json_mode where the model is biased towards producing a strict JSON blob and (2) function/tool calling where the model emits a canonical function call we can automatically parse and route to downstream services. both integrate with schema definitions and console validators.
[01:05] Ben: what does that look like in practice? like can it always output a valid JSON object?
[01:09] Priya: good question — in practice we combine prompting, temperature control, and a lightweight on-server validator that can run small repair passes or rejection sampling. so you'll get high probability of valid JSON; for strict pipelines we recommend function calling + server-side schema validation, plus a fallback policy.
[01:27] Alex: i'll demo a couple of examples — first the API JSON mode, then the console flow and Optimize tips to reduce flakiness in prod.
[01:34] [typing sounds]
[01:39] Priya: here's an example schema we use in the demo: order_id (string), amount (number), currency (enum), items (array of item objects with sku, qty), customer.contact.email (string). in the console you can paste an openapi-ish or json-schema and we auto-generate enforcement.
[01:57] Lina: curious about PII handling — if the model returns raw customer fields, how do we control retention?
[02:03] Jordan: good point — Redwood has configurable retention per-route, plus KMS integration for embeddings and optional token redaction. for private deployments we can keep logs in your VPC.
[02:14] Lina: ok thanks.
[02:16] [02:16] Priya: switching to live API demo — I'm going to call the JSON mode endpoint with a sample prompt: 'Extract invoice data into JSON according to schema'. temp set to 0.2, max tokens 300.
[02:31] [02:31] API response arrives]
[02:32] Priya: you can see the response — valid JSON, items array present. the console also highlights any schema mismatches. here we intentionally ask for an enum value not in schema and you can see the validator flagged it and the fallback policy triggered (we returned null for currency and emitted a validation error in the metadata).
[02:53] Mike: is the validator synchronous? do we wait on it before returning to caller?
[02:57] Priya: by default yes — validation happens server-side before the final response is returned. we offer a low-latency repair pass for small fixes. if you need hard real-time guarantees you can run function calls that bypass repair and instead return a structured call which your service executes.
[03:15] Alex: demoing function calling now — we'll show a function signature for create_payment(order_id, amount, currency, customer_email) and ask the model to 'call' the function with extracted args.
[03:28] [03:28] Priya: note — function calling is the most deterministic route. Redwood's runtime will produce a function_name + args blob; we validate args against the declared types and can either auto-invoke or hand off to the customer.
[03:41] Sara: can we prevent models from hallucinating function calls or inventing extra params?
[03:46] Priya: yes, the schema limits allowed params. we also have a 'deny-list' for unexpected keys and an allowlist mode. combined with low temp and calibration in Optimize you get very low incidence of hallucination.
[03:59] Ben: what's the ops path for when a function call fails? retries? compensation?
[04:04] Alex: typical pattern — Redwood emits the function call and metadata (confidence, token trace). your service returns success/failure and we can trigger retries or dead-letter. we also integrate tracing into the console so you can see the full request/response chain.
[04:21] [Screen: Console: Structured Output -> Schema Editor]
[04:25] Priya: showing the schema editor — you can paste a json-schema or create fields. we support enum suggestions, required flags, nested arrays. you can preview sample responses and run 'test prompts' in-console.
[04:40] Mike: does this feed into Optimize? can Optimize suggest changes to schema or prompt to reduce invalid outputs?
[04:46] Priya: Optimize doesn't change your schema automatically, but it analyzes prompt-response pairs, failure modes (like missing keys), and will recommend prompt templates, temperature settings, or small prompt augmentations. it also suggests batching profiles and quantization profiles for cost/latency tradeoffs.
[05:02] Jordan: for a production POC we'd typically run a small benchmark set (500-2k samples) and Optimize will recommend the model variant or quantization and an autoscaler config.
[05:13] [05:13] Sara: can you show a failing case?
[05:15] Priya: sure — here's an example where the model returns string 'two' for qty instead of integer. console flags it and the repair pass attempts to coerce; if it can't, it marks the field as invalid and the route policy decides whether to accept partials or reject.
[05:32] Mike: how do we monitor regressions over time?
[05:34] Priya: in Console you can attach eval sets and have continuous monitoring — any drop in schema match rate triggers alerts. we can integrate with Ops or Slack, and you can configure rollback policies by model version.
[05:47] Ben: what about multi-turn/assistant flows? we sometimes need chat flows that eventually produce a final JSON payload.
[05:54] Priya: supported — you can annotate the turn that should produce structured output, or use function calling mid-dialog. the runtime manages KV cache and context windows so the generation step has the relevant context.
[06:07] Lina: from a security perspective, access controls?
[06:09] Jordan: RBAC on routes, SSO (SAML), per-route encryption keys, audit logs. for Private deployments we offer HSM/KMS integration.
[06:17] [06:17] Alex: quick note on latency/cost: structured output with validation and repair adds a small CPU step; typical token latency is similar, but repair/validation can add ~10-60ms depending on complexity. Optimize can recommend a model variant/quant profile to reduce cost while keeping match rates.
[06:36] [Demo: function call -> auto-invoke -> shows downstream success]
[06:42] Priya: in this flow we auto-invoke a sample payment function — see the trace: request -> model -> function args -> service call -> success. the console shows confidence and token-level timing.
[06:55] Mike: can the function invocation happen inside a VPC in Dedicated or Private mode?
[06:59] Jordan: yes — for Dedicated we host service in your cloud VPC peering or Private we deploy in your VPC; function invocation can be routed via private endpoints.
[07:11] Sara: great. what's the recommended success criteria for a POC?
[07:14] Alex: typically 95% schema match on your eval set, latency within your SLO (e.g., p95 < 500ms), and throughput target met (x rps). also security signoffs — SOC2 checklist and network diagram.
[07:29] [07:29] Priya: moving to Optimize suggestions — here's a run on 1k samples: we recommended switching from large-llama-v2 to a quantized variant for 30% cost savings with ~1% drop in schema match; we also suggested increasing prefix caching on repeated invoice prompts which dropped p95 by 80ms.
[07:52] Mike: do you do automated prompt templating or we need to edit prompts by hand?
[07:55] Priya: Optimize will suggest templated prompts (examples) and you can A/B them via rollout settings in Console. it gives you candidate prompts and expected delta on metrics.
[08:06] Ben: curious about debugging — can we see token-level trace to find where the model went off-schema?
[08:11] Priya: yes token trace is in Console, and we surface the best/worst examples. we also show the exact prompt + response + schema diff.
[08:21] [08:21] Sara: how do you handle schema migrations if our product needs new fields later?
[08:25] Jordan: schema versioning in Console — you can stage a new schema, run a canary on 10% of traffic, and auto-fallback to previous version on regressions.
[08:36] Alex: quick live edit — I'll change schema to add 'customer.phone' optional and roll to 10% traffic.
[08:42] [08:42] [demo shows canary rollout and monitoring chart]
[08:46] Mike: nice, and if the model begins to hallucinate new fields we just reject?
[08:50] Priya: you can reject or map unknown keys to an 'extras' map depending on policy. mapping can be useful when you want to capture unknown but non-critical fields.
[08:59] [09:00] Ben: anything special about embeddings + structured output? we use embeddings for retrieval prior to extraction.
[09:05] Priya: retrieval + structured extraction is a common pattern. Redwood supports pinned context, and you can use retrieved chunks as part of the prompt. Optimize suggests caching hot retrievals to save tokens.
[09:18] Lina: any compliance notes for EU data residency?
[09:21] Jordan: yes we have region pinning and private deployments in EU regions; for strict residency we recommend Private deployment with local storage.
[09:29] Sara: what about error budgets during POC?
[09:31] Alex: we normally define an acceptable failure rate and set alert thresholds. we also provide a route-level SLA for Dedicated.
[09:38] [09:38] Priya: now quick Q&A from the demo code notebook — I'll paste the API call used. "POST /v1/responses" body includes input, json_schema, mode: 'json' and validation: 'strict'. sample response with 'validation_errors' object is returned in metadata.
[09:58] Mike: is there sample SDK code for common languages?
[10:01] Alex: yes we have node/python/java examples in the docs and the repo. I'll share the notebook.
[10:06] Ben: for function-calling auto-invoke into our systems, what's the auth model?
[10:10] Jordan: we support signed webhook endpoints, mTLS for private endpoints, and per-route API keys. for Dedicated/Private there's additional network controls.
[10:19] [10:19] Priya: last part — edge cases: long lists and very nested objects can sometimes exceed token limits. in those cases Optimize recommends streaming partial JSON or chunked extraction with reassembly. we demo a chunking pattern in the notebook.
[10:35] Sara: okay, that's helpful. any pricing ballpark for a small POC?
[10:38] Alex: ballpark — hosted API usage-based pricing; expect a small pilot under $5k/month depending on volume; Dedicated reserved capacity starts higher. I'll send a tailored proposal.
[10:51] Lina: can you include SOC2 + encryption details in that packet?
[10:53] Alex: yes will include SOC2 report and network whitepaper.
[10:56] [11:00] Ben: timeline — we'd like to start a 4-week POC in April if pricing looks good.
[11:06] Alex: sounds great, next steps we discussed: pricing + pilot proposal, demo notebook, SOC2 + arch docs, and schedule POC kickoff.
[11:16] [closing minutes with informal chatter and contact info exchange]
[11:25] Mike: thanks all, really useful demo.
[11:28] Alex: thanks team — we'll follow up with links.

Notes: shared artifacts: demo notebook link: https://redwood.ai/notebooks/structured-output-demo (demo only), security whitepaper link: https://redwood.ai/security/soc2, sample schema template: https://redwood.ai/docs/schemas.

End of transcript.
